1.title: Microsoft Sentinel Automation: Automation Rules and Playbooks
1.text: Welcome to Module five: Microsoft Sentinel Automation: Automation Rules and Playbooks. It covers the exam area one. Manage a security operations environment. Each part of this module comes from the study notes of the same name, so you can read the notes after you watch.

1.title: What You Will Learn
1.text: By the end of this module you will be able to do three things. Create and configure automation rules in Microsoft Sentinel. Create and configure Microsoft Sentinel playbooks. Practice with exam-style questions and a recall check.

1.title: Where This Fits in the Exam
1.text: Here is where this module sits in the exam. Exam area: one. Manage a security operations environment (forty to forty-five percent). Exam format: one hundred minutes; a score of seven hundred on a scale of one to one thousand passes. Validated against: the official Microsoft S C-two hundred study guide and Microsoft Learn.

1.title: Automation rules
1.text: Automation rules. The figure shows this: An automation rule runs its actions in order; one action can start a playbook.

1.title: Automation rules, continued
1.text: Automation rules. An automation rule is a centralized, rule-based way to handle incidents and alerts without code. It has a trigger, conditions and actions. Triggers. When incident is created, When incident is updated, When alert is created (alert trigger only for Scheduled, N R T and Microsoft security analytics rules). Conditions. equals or does not equal, contains, starts with, ends with (and their negations); the update trigger adds changed, changed from, changed to, added. Actions. Add task, change status (closing reason and comment when closing), change severity, assign owner, add tag, run playbook.

1.title: Automation rules, continued
1.text: Automation rules. The condition Updated by can be Application, User, A I R, Alert grouping, Playbook, Automation rule or Other. Tag conditions can match any individual tag or the collection of all tags. Exam tip: Use automation rules for simple, high-volume tasks (assign, tag, close, set severity). Use a playbook only when you need an external system or logic.

1.title: Order and timing
1.text: Order and timing. Order number. Sets execution order; lowest runs first. Queues. Each trigger type has its own queue; created-trigger rules run before updated-trigger rules. Same number. Rules with equal order run in random order; the portal does not stop duplicates. Actions inside a rule. Run in the listed order. Playbook wait. Under one s: the next action runs at once; under two minutes: next action within two minutes of the start; longer: next action at two minutes. Expiration date. The rule is disabled after that date; ideal for penetration test noise. Exam tip: Use an expiration date for a temporary rule, for example closing incidents from a scheduled penetration test. It turns itself off.

1.title: Where automation rules are created
1.text: Where automation rules are created. Automation page, then Automation rules tab. Main place; in the Defender portal under Microsoft Sentinel, then Configuration, then Automation. Analytics rule wizard, then Automated response tab. Bound to that analytics rule. Incidents page. Pre-filled from an incident; suggests suppression and expiration (Azure portal only). Rules can be exported and imported as A R M (Azure Resource Manager) Jason. In the Defender portal, alert-trigger rules act on Sentinel alerts; Microsoft incident creation rules are not supported; changes within five to ten minutes are batched into one update, and an incident from Defender can take up to ten minutes to reach a rule.

1.title: Playbooks
1.text: Playbooks. A playbook is a collection of steps built on Azure Logic Apps, either Consumption or Standard (extra charges apply). Automation rules can run both types. Microsoft Sentinel incident. Recommended; receives the incident with its alerts and entities; attach it to an automation rule. Microsoft Sentinel alert (preview). Manual runs on alerts, or rules that create no incidents. Microsoft Sentinel entity. Manual runs on an entity during an investigation or hunt. Common actions: Get incident, Update incident (status, owner, tags, severity, title, description), Add comment to incident, and Entities actions (get I P, host, account, U R L, file hash). Updating needs the incident A R M I D. Manual runs on alerts and on entities are not supported in the Defender portal.

1.title: Permissions
1.text: Permissions. Sentinel service account that runs playbooks from an automation rule. Microsoft Sentinel Automation Contributor on the playbook's resource group; granting it needs Owner (portal link Manage playbook permissions). Analyst who runs a playbook manually. Microsoft Sentinel Responder (open the incident) plus Microsoft Sentinel Playbook Operator. Engineer who attaches a playbook to a rule. Microsoft Sentinel Contributor. Person who edits a playbook. Logic App Contributor (Standard: Logic Apps Standard Contributor or Developer). Person who may only enable or disable. Logic App Operator.

1.title: Authenticating a playbook to Sentinel
1.text: Authenticating a playbook to Sentinel. Managed identity. Enable system-assigned identity on the Logic App, then assign it a role on the workspace: Microsoft Sentinel Responder to update incidents, Reader to only receive them. Service principal. Entra app; client I D, tenant and secret; Microsoft Sentinel Contributor to write, Reader to read. Entra user. Signs in with a user account. Assigning roles needs Owner or User Access Administrator. Exam tip: Read or trigger equals Reader. Write (update incident, add comment) equals Responder or Contributor. Prefer a managed identity over a secret.

1.title: Practice Question 1
1.text: Question one. A sock wants every incident created by one specific analytics rule to be assigned to the Tier one group automatically, with no code. What should be built? The four options are on the screen. The answer is B: An automation rule triggered on incident creation that assigns an owner. An automation rule with the incident created trigger can filter by analytics rule and assign an owner.

1.title: Practice Question 2
1.text: Question two. An automation rule must run a playbook, but the run is denied. What is the most likely missing permission? The four options are on the screen. The answer is A: Microsoft Sentinel Automation Contributor on the playbook resource group. The Sentinel service account needs Microsoft Sentinel Automation Contributor on the playbook's resource group, and Owner is needed to grant it.

1.title: Practice Question 3
1.text: Question three. A company runs a two-week penetration test that will create many incidents. The sock wants them closed automatically and the rule to stop after the test. Which setting helps? The four options are on the screen. The answer is B: An expiration date on an automation rule that closes the incidents. An automation rule with an expiration date disables itself after that date.

1.title: Practice Question 4
1.text: Question four. Two automation rules use the incident created trigger with order numbers ten and twenty. A third uses the incident updated trigger with order one. Which statement is correct? The four options are on the screen. The answer is C: The created-trigger rules run first, in order ten and then twenty. Each trigger type has its own queue, and created-trigger rules run before updated-trigger rules.

1.title: Practice Question 5
1.text: Question five. A playbook that uses a system-assigned managed identity must update the status of incidents. Which role should be assigned to the identity on the workspace? The four options are on the screen. The answer is C: Microsoft Sentinel Responder, which can update incidents. Updating incidents needs Responder (or Contributor); Reader only receives incidents.

1.title: Practice Question 6
1.text: Question six. A junior analyst must open incidents and run playbooks manually, with the least privilege. Which roles should be assigned? The four options are on the screen. The answer is D: Microsoft Sentinel Responder and Microsoft Sentinel Playbook Operator. Responder opens the incident and Playbook Operator runs the playbook manually.

1.title: Recall Check 1
1.text: Recall check one. Say each answer out loud before you listen to mine. Question one. Which Sentinel trigger is recommended for playbooks? Answer: Microsoft Sentinel incident. Question two. Which service are playbooks built on? Answer: Azure Logic Apps (Consumption or Standard). Question three. Which role lets Sentinel run playbooks from automation rules? Answer: Microsoft Sentinel Automation Contributor, on the playbook's resource group.

1.title: Recall Check 2
1.text: Recall check two. Say each answer out loud before you listen to mine. Question four. Which automation rules run first? Answer: Created-trigger rules, before updated-trigger rules, lowest order number first. Question five. Which action sets a closing reason? Answer: Change status. Question six. Where is the Sentinel automation page in the Defender portal? Answer: Microsoft Sentinel, then Configuration, then Automation.

1.title: Module Recap
1.text: Here is the recap. Automation rule: trigger, conditions, actions; order number; expiration date. Triggers: incident created, incident updated, alert created. Actions: add task, change status, change severity, assign owner, add tag, run playbook. Playbook: Logic Apps; incident trigger recommended. Run from rule: Automation Contributor on the playbook resource group (Owner grants it). Manual run: Responder plus Playbook Operator. Playbook identity: Reader to receive, Responder or Contributor to write.
